title: T1566.001 — Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: Animated simulation of a spearphishing attachment attack

steps.title: WHAT IS HAPPENING NOW Step 1 - Pick the target
steps.caption: The attacker researches people at the target company. Public websites and social media reveal that Jane works in accounts payable and handles invoices. Her email address is easy to guess. This first step is called reconnaissance. WHAT DEFENDERS CAN SEE
steps.defender: Defenders see nothing yet. But public information about your staff is the attacker's first weapon - reduce what you publish, and train teams to be careful with work details online.

fields.detail: WHAT IS HAPPENING NOW Step 1 - Pick the target The attacker researches people at the target company.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: WHAT IS HAPPENING NOW Step 2 - Build the malicious file
steps.caption: The attacker creates a document that looks like a normal invoice. Inside it hides a macro - a small program that runs when the file opens and macros are enabled. The icon is changed to look like a PDF, so fewer people suspect it. WHAT DEFENDERS CAN SEE
steps.defender: Nothing to see on your network yet. But Threat Intelligence can catch the campaign early: some mailboxes elsewhere in the world receive the same file first, and feeds report it.

steps.title: WHAT IS HAPPENING NOW Step 3 - Send the spearphishing e
steps.caption: mail The attacker sends the email from a server they control. It pretends to come from a known supplier, and the subject line creates pressure: "Overdue invoice". The attachment carries the malicious document. WHAT DEFENDERS CAN SEE
steps.defender: Email gateway logs show a new sender domain, a failed DMARC check, and a macro document type. This is your first real chance to stop the attack - a rule like R4 fires here.

steps.title: WHAT IS HAPPENING NOW Step 4
steps.caption: The email lands in the inbox The gateway lets the message pass - the file has no known bad signature, so automated checks see nothing famous. The email now sits in Jane's inbox, next to real invoices. WHAT DEFENDERS CAN SEE
steps.defender: Mail logs still record the delivery: sender, attachment name, recipients. Teach users to report with one click - a report at this moment costs nothing.

steps.title: WHAT IS HAPPENING NOW Step 5
steps.caption: The user opens the email Jane sees a normal invoice email. She is busy, and the message copies the supplier's real style, so it looks familiar. She clicks the attachment to view the invoice. WHAT DEFENDERS CAN SEE
steps.defender: Users click. That is not stupidity - it is human nature under time pressure. Plan for the click: the defense lines that matter come next.

steps.title: WHAT IS HAPPENING NOW Step 6 - Macros are enabled
steps.caption: The document opens. Office shows a yellow bar: "Enable Content". Jane only wants to see the invoice, so she clicks it. The hidden macro now runs with Jane's permissions. WHAT DEFENDERS CAN SEE
steps.defender: The policy "Block macros from the internet" stops this step automatically. Files from email carry a Mark of the Web, and Office can simply refuse to run their macros.

steps.title: WHAT IS HAPPENING NOW Step 7 - Office spawns a shell Th
steps.caption: e macro starts PowerShell, a built-in Windows tool, and hides its window. Word (WINWORD.EXE) is now the parent of PowerShell - something normal office software never does. The attacker has code execution. WHAT DEFENDERS CAN SEE
steps.defender: This is the strongest detection of the whole technique: an Office process creating a command-line child. Sysmon Event ID 1 and EDR show it clearly - Sigma rule R1 fires here.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: WHAT IS HAPPENING NOW Step 8
steps.caption: The real payload is downloaded PowerShell downloads the second stage - the actual malware - from the attacker's server, then runs it. Much of it stays in memory, so antivirus on disk finds little. WHAT DEFENDERS CAN SEE
steps.defender: Proxy and DNS logs reveal a brand-new domain and a PowerShell user agent fetching a script. Sigma rules R2 and R5 catch exactly this behavior.
